body.objective: Students will be able to use stage areas and directions.
body.iCan: I can use stage areas and directions.
successCriteria: I can name the nine stage areas
I can follow and write blocking using stage directions
I can move on stage so the audience can see and hear me
body.hook: Imagine a scene where the most important moment happens with the actor's back to the audience. Nobody sees it. Blocking, the planned movement of actors on stage, makes sure the audience sees what matters.

study.title: Map the Stage
study.question: How do actors use stage areas and blocking so the audience can follow the story?
study.passage:
Stage map (proscenium stage): The stage is divided into nine areas, named from the actor's point of view facing the audience:
Upstage Right (UR) | Upstage Centre (UC) | Upstage Left (UL)
Centre Right (CR) | Centre (C) | Centre Left (CL)
Downstage Right (DR) | Downstage Centre (DC) | Downstage Left (DL)
Why "upstage"? Old stages were raked (sloped up away from the audience), so walking away meant walking up.
Activity 1, Stage director says (10 minutes): The teacher calls areas; everyone moves there. Speed up.
Activity 2, Blocking notation (10 minutes): Learn shorthand: X = cross, DSL = downstage left, Ent. = enter, Ex. = exit. Example: "X DL to window" means cross to downstage left to the window.
Activity 3, Block a scene (25 minutes): In pairs, take a short two-person scene. Write blocking in the margin for each line. Rules: strongest moments downstage or centre; cheat out; don't stand in a straight line with your partner; motivate every move. Run it for another pair who checks sightlines.
study.source: Original activities written for this lesson; stage terminology from standard theatre practice.
steps: Block a short scene in the script margin
discussion: Why are stage directions given from the actor's view, not the audience's?
Where on stage do moments feel strongest? Why?
What makes a move feel motivated rather than random?
How did cheating out change what the audience could see?
study.product: Perform a blocked two-person scene of about two minutes and submit the script with blocking notation and motivations in the margin.

examples.title: Stage left
examples.problem: You face the audience and step to your left. Which way did you go?
examples.explore: Which side is that for the audience?

examples.title: Upstage
examples.problem: Why is the back of the stage called upstage?
examples.answer: Old stages sloped upward away from the audience
examples.explore: What does it mean to "upstage" another actor?

examples.title: Notation
examples.answer: Enter from upstage right and cross to downstage centre

examples.title: Cheat out
examples.problem: Two actors talk face to face in profile. How do you improve the sightline?
examples.answer: Both cheat out, turning partly to the audience
examples.explore: How far can you turn and still seem to talk to each other?

practice.q: Write notation for "cross to upstage left."
Why should every move be motivated?
practice.a: A reason makes it believable and purposeful.

practice.q: Why avoid standing in a straight line with your partner?
practice.a: It looks flat and can block sightlines.

practice.q: Why are strong moments often placed downstage centre?
practice.a: It is closest and most visible to the audience.

practice.q: What does it mean to "upstage" someone?
practice.a: To move upstage so they must turn their back to the audience to face you.

practice.q: How would blocking change on a thrust stage?
practice.a: Audience on three sides, so actors move more to share sightlines.

practice.q: Give a motivation for crossing DL during a scene about bad news.
practice.a: For example, turning away to hide tears.

misconceptions: Thinking stage left is the audience's left
Turning your back to the audience during important lines
exitTicket: Write blocking notation for entering stage right and crossing to centre.

items.q: What is cheating out and why do actors do it?
items.answer: Turning partly to the audience so they can be seen and heard.
So movement is believable and supports the story.

items.q: Explain where you would place the most important moment of a scene and why.
items.answer: Downstage centre or a strong position so the audience sees it clearly.
It focuses attention, shows relationships and reveals character.
